title: Caching & Performance Tuning
summary: Databases are fast — until they're not. Learn where caches live, how writes flow through them, why invalidation is the hard part, and how indexes and EXPLAIN turn slow queries fast.

blocks.markdown:
A **cache** is a fast, small store that holds copies of expensive results so later reads skip the original source.

- Cuts **latency** — answer from memory in microseconds vs milliseconds from disk.
- Cuts **database load** — the same popular row needn't hit the DB a thousand times a second.
- Every caching decision involves a tradeoff: speed vs **staleness**.
- Tuning means finding and removing the bottleneck: index gaps, slow queries, overloaded connections.

Database disk I/O is the dominant latency source in most web apps.

- **Memory** access: ~100 ns. **SSD** read: ~100 µs. **HDD** read: ~10 ms — 100,000× slower than memory.
- A cache holds **hot data** (the 20% of rows read 80% of the time) in RAM.
- Result: the DB handles far fewer reads, query load drops, and p99 latency shrinks dramatically.

Caching is always the first lever to pull before scaling hardware.

Caches exist at every layer of the stack, each closer to the user than the last.

- A request stops at the first layer that has the answer.
- Each layer has its own eviction policy and invalidation challenge.

blocks.subTitle: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
blocks.markdown:
**Cache-aside** is the most common read strategy. The application owns the cache explicitly.

1. **Check cache.** If found (**cache hit**), return it.
2. **On miss,** query the database.
3. **Write the result into the cache**, then return it.

- The cache only ever holds data that has actually been requested — no wasted space.
- Downside: the **first request always misses**; a cold start floods the DB.
- If the cache crashes, the app keeps working (falls back to DB).

Used by: Redis + most web frameworks.

blocks.subTitle: Write-through
blocks.markdown:
**Write-through** writes to the cache and the database **simultaneously** (synchronously) on every update.

- Cache is always in sync with the DB — **no stale data**.
- Writes are **slow**: the caller waits for both the cache write and the DB write to complete.
- Good for data that is **read often and updated occasionally** (user profile, product catalog).

Trade-off: strong consistency, higher write latency.

blocks.subTitle: Write-back (write-behind)
blocks.markdown:
**Write-back** (also called **write-behind**) writes to the cache immediately and flushes to the DB **asynchronously** later.

- Writes feel instant to the caller — **low write latency**.
- Risk: if the cache crashes before the flush, **data is lost**.
- Best for write-heavy workloads where some data loss is tolerable (analytics counters, game scores).

Trade-off: fast writes, durability risk.

blocks.subTitle: Write-around
blocks.markdown:
**Write-around** bypasses the cache entirely on writes — data goes straight to the DB.

- The cache is populated only on the next read miss (cache-aside style).
- Prevents cache pollution when data is written but rarely re-read (bulk imports, log ingestion).
- New writes will cause a **cache miss** on the very next read — a deliberate trade-off.

Trade-off: avoids pointless cache churn; costs one extra DB read on first access.

blocks.subTitle: Strategy comparison
blocks.markdown:
Pick the write strategy by your durability and latency needs.

| Strategy | Write speed | Data loss risk |
|---|---|---|
| Write-through | Slow (sync both) | No |
| Write-back | Fast (async flush) | Yes |
| Write-around | DB speed (bypass) | No |

Write-through is the safe default; write-back only when write throughput is the bottleneck.

**Cache invalidation** is removing or updating a cached entry when the underlying data changes. Phil Karlton famously called it one of the two hard problems in CS.

- **TTL (time-to-live):** cache entries expire automatically after N seconds. Simple but imprecise — data may be stale until expiry.
- **Event-driven invalidation:** the application explicitly deletes or updates the cache key when it writes to the DB. Precise but complex to implement.
- **Problem:** distributed systems with multiple cache nodes make invalidation even harder — some nodes may hold the old value.

Most systems use TTL as a safety net plus event-driven invalidation for critical data.

A **cache stampede** (thundering herd) happens when a popular cache entry expires and hundreds of concurrent requests all miss simultaneously — all racing to regenerate the same value from the DB.

- The DB receives a sudden spike of identical queries, potentially crashing it.
- **Mitigations:**
  - **Mutex / lock:** only one thread regenerates; others wait.
  - **Probabilistic early expiry:** renew the entry slightly before it expires, based on random chance — smooths regeneration over time.
  - **Background refresh:** a worker refreshes popular keys before they expire, serving stale data for a brief window.

See [sharding-replication-scaling](sharding-replication-scaling) for high-availability context.

The **N+1 problem** occurs when code fetches a list of N items, then issues one extra query per item to load related data — N+1 queries total.

Example: fetch 100 orders (1 query), then for each order fetch its customer (100 queries) = 101 round trips.

- Root cause: lazy loading in an ORM that isn't told to batch.
- **Fix: eager loading / JOIN.** Fetch orders and customers together in one query using a JOIN, or use the ORM's batch-load feature (`includes`, `preload`, `eager_load` in Rails; `select_related` in Django).
- Also curable by caching the per-item lookups in the application layer.

See [query-processing-optimization](query-processing-optimization).

A **connection pool** is a set of pre-opened database connections that are reused across application requests instead of opening a new connection per request.

- Opening a TCP connection + authenticating takes ~5–50 ms. Under load this adds up.
- A pool keeps N connections open; incoming requests borrow one, use it, and return it.
- **Pool exhaustion:** if all connections are in use, new requests queue or fail. Set pool size to match your DB's max connections.

Tools: PgBouncer (Postgres), HikariCP (Java), connection pool built into most ORMs.

An **index** is a separate data structure (usually a B-tree) that maps column values to row locations, enabling lookups in O(log n) instead of O(n) full scans.

- **Add an index** on every column used in WHERE, JOIN ON, or ORDER BY that causes slow queries.
- **Composite index:** index on (a, b) helps queries filtering on a alone or on (a, b), but not on b alone — column order matters.
- **Too many indexes** slow writes (every INSERT/UPDATE must update each index).
- **Covering index:** index includes all columns the query needs — the DB answers entirely from the index without touching the table.

See [indexing](indexing) for the full picture.

blocks.sectionTitle: Using EXPLAIN to find slow queries
blocks.markdown:
`EXPLAIN` (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in Postgres/MySQL) shows the **query execution plan** the DB chose — the sequence of operations it will perform.

- Look for **Seq Scan** on large tables — the DB is reading every row; an index is likely missing.
- **Rows** estimates vs actual: large gaps mean stale statistics; run `ANALYZE` to refresh.
- **Cost** is a unitless estimate (lower is better).
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually **runs the query** and shows real timings — don't use on mutations in production without a transaction rollback.

EXPLAIN is the first tool to reach for when a query is slow.

blocks.sectionTitle: Using EXPLAIN to find slow queries
blocks.subTitle: Reading the plan
blocks.markdown:
A minimal EXPLAIN workflow in Postgres:

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
```

Output (simplified):
```
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..3412.00 rows=1 width=64)
                    (actual time=0.042..18.321 rows=1 loops=1)
```

`Seq Scan` = no index used; add one:
```sql
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
```

After indexing the plan shows `Index Scan` and actual time drops from ~18 ms to ~0.1 ms.

Common caching and performance mistakes:

- **Caching mutable data without a TTL** — stale entries live forever; users see wrong data.
- **Caching too aggressively** — invalidation logic gets out of sync; bugs appear only in production.
- **Ignoring cache hit rate** — if hit rate is below ~80% the cache isn't helping; re-examine what you cache.
- **Over-indexing** — every index slows writes; index only columns that appear in real slow queries.
- **Not pooling connections** — at scale, connection setup time dominates; always use a pool.

blocks.subTitle: Cache-aside vs write-through
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between cache-aside and write-through?**

**Cache-aside** is a read strategy: the app checks the cache on every read and populates it on a miss. The cache is never written to on a write — the DB is updated directly.

**Write-through** is a write strategy: every write goes to the cache and the DB simultaneously, keeping them in sync.

They're often combined: cache-aside for reads + write-through for writes gives strong consistency with lazy population.

blocks.subTitle: The N+1 problem
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the N+1 query problem and how do you fix it?**

Fetching a list of N items then querying once per item for related data — N+1 round trips instead of 1.

**Fix:** use a JOIN or the ORM's eager-load feature to fetch all related data in a single query. For example, in Rails replace `Order.all` (then lazy `.customer`) with `Order.includes(:customer).all`.

Spot it with a query counter or slow-query log — you'll see the same query repeated N times.

blocks.subTitle: Cache invalidation
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How do you handle cache invalidation?**

Three main approaches:
- **TTL:** entries expire automatically after N seconds — simple but allows a stale window.
- **Event-driven:** the application deletes or updates the cache key whenever it writes to the DB — precise but must be wired into every write path.
- **Versioning:** cache keys include a version number; a new version key is written on update, and old keys naturally fall off via TTL.

In practice: use TTL as a safety net and event-driven deletion for data that must be fresh.

blocks.subTitle: Cache stampede
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?**

When a hot cache entry expires, many concurrent threads simultaneously miss and all query the DB at once — a thundering herd.

**Prevention:**
- **Mutex:** only one thread regenerates; others wait or return stale data.
- **Background refresh:** a worker renews the key before expiry; readers always see a (briefly stale) value.
- **Probabilistic early expiry (XFetch):** each request has a small chance of early regeneration, spreading the load over time.

blocks.subTitle: Connection pooling
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why use connection pooling?**

Opening a DB connection requires a TCP handshake and authentication — ~5–50 ms each. Under load, that overhead dominates.

A pool pre-opens N connections and reuses them. Requests borrow a connection, execute, and return it in milliseconds. Without a pool, a 1000 req/s workload would attempt 1000 new connections per second — most DBs cap out well below that.

Set pool size just below the DB's max connection limit; too large and the DB itself becomes the bottleneck.
